name: Agriculture
blurb: Vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, and autonomous equipment at commercial scale, tracked through USDA ERS, FAO, satellite data providers, and the equipment and standards bodies.

points.desc: Deere's precision agriculture line (See and Spray, autonomous tractors) is the reference commercial deployment.
points.name: Precision ag is shipping product

points.desc: Census BTOS covers agriculture-adjacent sectors in its fortnightly AI-use series.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The Economic Research Service publishes the data series on precision-agriculture adoption across US farms - variable-rate technology, yield monitoring, autonomous equipment. The federal measurement layer.
points.name: USDA ERS measures US adoption

points.desc: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's digital agriculture program, with the 60 Decibels-supported Digital Agriculture Index, benchmarks platform adoption and real-world yield and income impact.
points.name: FAO benchmarks digital agriculture globally

points.desc: The AgriFoodTech investment research tracks venture capital into agricultural AI, robotics, computer vision, and farm-management software - the sector's funding barometer.
points.name: AgFunder indexes the investment flow

points.desc: Planet Labs' high-resolution imagery, Descartes Labs' geospatial ML, and EarthDaily's field-level crop indicators supply the AI-ready observation data behind yield prediction and crop-stress detection.
points.name: The satellite layer feeds the models

points.desc: The Association of Equipment Manufacturers covers autonomous machinery, AI hardware standards, and robotics adoption across crop and livestock production.
points.name: AEM tracks the machinery standards

points.desc: The nonprofit consortium sets the open data standards that let AI models ingest feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites - the plumbing under everything else.
points.name: AgGateway makes the data interoperable

points.desc: The International Society of Precision Agriculture is the scientific organization connecting academic research on remote sensing and spatial analytics to commercial practice.
points.name: ISPA bridges the science and the field

points.desc: The 100 Million Farmers initiative tracks AI adoption through the lens of climate-smart and regenerative agriculture metrics globally.
points.name: WEF tracks climate-smart adoption

points.desc: Bayer's Climate FieldView and Corteva's Granular are the large digital-farming platforms turning soil, weather, and yield data into planting and input prescriptions with machine learning.
points.name: The agribusiness platforms run the prescriptions

points.desc: CNH Industrial's Raven division builds driverless tractor technology, AI path-planning, and precision application - the equipment layer beyond Deere.
points.name: CNH and Raven automate the other fleets

points.desc: Carbon Robotics' LaserWeeder kills weeds with computer vision and lasers instead of herbicide; Monarch builds electric driverless tractors - narrow AI shipping as farm equipment.
points.name: The pure-plays attack single problems

summary: Precision agriculture - vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, autonomous equipment - is deployed at commercial scale. Who tracks it: federal adoption data, a UN benchmarking framework, a venture index, and standards bodies, layered over the equipment giants and AI pure-plays actually shipping it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey previously recorded 13.7% of agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting firms answering yes to using AI in the prior survey period, though the most recent figure has been suppressed. That single number understates the texture of what is actually being deployed, because AI in agriculture arrives bundled inside machinery, platform subscriptions, and satellite data services rather than as a discrete software purchase that farmers easily recognize and report.

The clearest commercial deployments sit inside precision agriculture equipment and digital farming platforms. Carbon Robotics describes itself as the leader in physical AI for agriculture, with its LaserWeeder guided by what the company calls a Large Plant Model trained on the world's largest agricultural dataset collected by its machines in the field. The system uses computer vision to identify and destroy weeds with lasers rather than herbicide, and it can be switched between manual and autonomous operation. On the data side, Climate FieldView reports that farmers using its AI-generated seed scripts saw an average increase of plus five bushels per acre compared to users who wrote their own scripts, which is one of the more concrete yield-impact figures available from a commercial platform. Planet Labs supplies the satellite observation layer that feeds these and similar models, offering daily high-resolution Earth imagery combined with analytics tools through its Planet Insights Platform.

Investment flows give a sense of where capital is concentrating. AgFunder, which tracks venture funding into agrifoodtech startups, reported that global agrifoodtech funding reached 16 billion dollars in 2024, a four percent drop from 2023, and hit 16.2 billion dollars in 2025, nearly flat at negative three percent versus the prior year. Investors are, per AgFunder, writing checks more selectively and directing capital toward companies with tangible science, real unit economics, and clear paths to revenue. Regional patterns are uneven: Asia-Pacific agrifoodtech startups raised 4.2 billion dollars through October 2024, a 38 percent increase over the same period in 2023, while African agrifoodtech raised 145 million dollars in the first half of 2024, a 1.6 percent year-over-year increase but still representing just 1.6 percent of global investment. Developing markets overall saw agrifoodtech funding grow 63 percent between 2023 and 2024, contrasting with the four percent global decline.

The infrastructure supporting AI in agriculture depends on interoperability and data standards that most farmers never see directly. AgGateway, a nonprofit consortium, works to enable digital connectivity across agriculture by developing the resources and relationships that let data move between tractors, drones, soil sensors, satellites, and farm management platforms. The International Society of Precision Agriculture connects academic remote sensing and spatial analytics research to commercial practice and has published its precision agriculture definition in over fifteen languages. The Association of Equipment Manufacturers brings together agricultural original equipment manufacturers to shape policy, understand data, and develop strategies on issues including autonomous machinery. The Food and Agriculture Organization has launched programs including the Innovate Africa Challenge in partnership with Smart Africa to accelerate adoption of AI solutions addressing agricultural and climate challenges on that continent.

For an operator evaluating whether to deploy, the honest picture is one of uneven but real commercial results concentrated in specific task categories: weed control, variable-rate input application, and yield prediction. The ROI evidence that exists, such as the plus-five-bushels-per-acre figure from Climate FieldView, is self-reported by vendors and applies to users of particular platform features rather than to broad farm populations. Investment has cooled from earlier peaks and is consolidating around companies that can demonstrate unit economics. The measurement infrastructure, from USDA's Economic Research Service to the Census Bureau survey, is still catching up to how bundled AI actually enters farm operations, which means adoption statistics should be read cautiously. The data standards work being done by organizations like AgGateway matters considerably, because AI models are only as useful as the quality and compatibility of the sensor and field data fed into them.
